subject: anthropology
topicDisplay: Hl Essay Reflexive Engagement With Anthropology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Gramsci's neo-Marxist concept of 'hegemony' refers to:
options: Rule maintained purely through physical force
The complete absence of ruling-class power
The economic base determining everything mechanically
Ideological and moral leadership by which the ruling class wins consent to its dominance
questions.explain: Gramsci argued the ruling class maintains power partly through hegemony, securing the consent of the subordinate class via ideas and culture.

questions.q: Interpretivists object to a positivist science of society because they argue that:
options: Human behaviour is meaningful and cannot be reduced to measurable external causes
Statistics are always perfectly accurate
Society has no patterns at all
Objectivity is easily achieved through experiments
questions.explain: Interpretivists hold that, unlike matter, humans have consciousness and meanings, so social life must be understood rather than merely measured.

questions.q: The New Right perspective on sociology and social policy typically argues that:
options: Generous welfare creates a 'dependency culture' and undermines self-reliance
Capitalism is the sole cause of crime
Social and Cultural Anthropology should never influence policy
State welfare should be expanded to eliminate poverty
questions.explain: New Right thinkers such as Murray argue over-generous welfare fosters dependency and an underclass, favouring reduced state intervention.

questions.q: Positivists tend to favour social surveys and questionnaires because they:
options: Are reliable, produce quantifiable data and allow comparisons and correlations
Cannot be replicated
Generate rich, in-depth qualitative meanings
Always achieve perfect validity
questions.explain: Positivists value questionnaires for their reliability, large samples and standardised quantitative data that can reveal patterns and correlations.

questions.q: Parsons compared society to a biological organism. In this analogy, social institutions are like:
options: Isolated cells with no connection
Random external shocks
Interdependent organs each meeting a functional need of the whole
Competing predators
questions.explain: Parsons' organic analogy treats institutions as interdependent parts that each contribute to the survival and equilibrium of the social system.

questions.q: Difference feminism criticises other feminist perspectives for:
options: Focusing too much on individual women's experiences
Ignoring biological differences entirely
Treating 'women' as a single category and overlooking differences of ethnicity, class and sexuality
Rejecting all forms of patriarchy
questions.explain: Difference feminists argue that women's experiences vary by class, ethnicity and sexuality, so a single account of patriarchy is inadequate.

questions.q: Karl Popper argued that the key criterion distinguishing science from non-science is:
options: Verification by repeated observation
The use of large data samples
Consensus among experts
Falsifiability: scientific statements must be capable of being proved false
questions.explain: Popper argued that genuinely scientific theories make bold, testable predictions that can in principle be falsified by evidence.

questions.q: Functionalism is best described as a consensus theory because it assumes:
options: Individual meanings are the only social reality
Society depends on shared norms and values that integrate its members
All social institutions serve the ruling class
Society is based on inevitable class conflict
questions.explain: Functionalists such as Durkheim and Parsons see society as held together by a value consensus that socialises members into agreed norms.

questions.q: The practical, ethical and theoretical (PET) factors affecting choice of method include which practical consideration?
options: The time, funding and access available to the researcher
Informed consent of participants
The validity of the data
The researcher's theoretical perspective
questions.explain: Practical factors include time, money, funding, access to subjects and the personal characteristics of the researcher.

questions.q: Postmodernists such as Lyotard argue that society has moved beyond modernity, characterised by:
options: The triumph of positivist science as absolute truth
A return to traditional religion as the sole truth
Incredulity towards meta-narratives, fragmentation and diversity
Growing confidence in single 'meta-narratives' like Marxism
questions.explain: Lyotard defined the postmodern as incredulity towards the grand meta-narratives that once claimed to explain the whole of society.

questions.q: Traditional Marxism is a conflict theory because it argues that society is fundamentally shaped by:
options: Individual rational choices in a free market
The interpretive meanings actors attach to action
The exploitative relationship between the bourgeoisie and the proletariat
A shared value consensus
questions.explain: Marx argued that the economic base, founded on class exploitation, shapes the superstructure and generates inherent class conflict.

questions.q: The positivist position on whether sociology can be a science holds that:
options: Social and Cultural Anthropology can use scientific methods to discover observable, quantifiable social facts and causal laws
Only empathetic understanding reveals truth
Science and sociology are entirely incompatible
Society cannot be measured objectively at all
questions.explain: Positivists like Durkheim argued that sociology can study observable social facts objectively and uncover law-like causal patterns.

questions.q: Liberal feminism is distinctive in arguing that gender inequality can be reduced mainly through:
options: Abolishing the capitalist economy first
Rejecting any idea of progress
The violent overthrow of patriarchy
Gradual reform, legal change and challenging gender socialisation
questions.explain: Liberal feminists believe equality can be achieved progressively through legal reform, equal opportunities and changing socialisation.

questions.q: The debate over 'objectivity and values' in sociology concerns whether:
options: Crime is functional
Society is based on consensus or conflict
Sociologists can and should keep their own values out of their research
Social and Cultural Anthropology should use questionnaires or interviews
questions.explain: Sociologists disagree over whether value-freedom is possible or desirable, with Weber, Gouldner and others taking differing positions.

questions.q: Interpretivists generally prefer unstructured interviews because they:
options: Yield valid, in-depth qualitative data about respondents' meanings
Eliminate all interviewer bias
Are the cheapest method available
Produce easily quantifiable, reliable data
questions.explain: Unstructured interviews allow rapport and flexibility, generating valid insight into how respondents see and interpret their world.

questions.q: Official statistics are described by interpretivists as 'social constructs' because they argue that:
options: Only positivists collect them
They contain no quantitative data
Statistics are always completely accurate
The figures are produced through decisions and definitions of officials, not simply objective facts
questions.explain: Interpretivists such as Atkinson argue statistics reflect the labelling and recording decisions of officials rather than a neutral mirror of reality.

questions.q: Thomas Kuhn's concept of a 'paradigm' suggests that a discipline is a mature science when:
options: Its findings are always subjective
It is dominated by a single accepted framework that guides 'normal science'
It cannot be falsified
It rejects all shared assumptions
questions.explain: Kuhn argued a science is unified by a paradigm of shared assumptions; on this basis some claim sociology is 'pre-paradigmatic'.

questions.q: In assessing documents as a secondary source, Scott's four criteria are authenticity, credibility, representativeness and:
options: Meaning
Cost
Falsifiability
Reliability
questions.explain: John Scott proposed judging documents by authenticity, credibility, representativeness and meaning (their interpretation and significance).

questions.q: Among ethical factors in research, 'informed consent' requires that:
options: The state approves the findings
Participants agree to take part with full knowledge of the study's nature and purpose
Researchers conceal the aims to avoid bias
Only quantitative data is collected
questions.explain: Informed consent means participants are told what the research involves and agree freely, a core ethical principle alongside confidentiality and avoiding harm.

questions.q: Symbolic interactionism, associated with Mead and Blumer, holds that:
options: Behaviour is wholly determined by social structures
People act towards things on the basis of the meanings those things have for them
Society exists independently of human interaction
Only quantitative data reveals social reality
questions.explain: Interactionists argue that meaning is created and negotiated through interaction, and that the self develops through taking the role of others.

questions.q: Which type of feminism argues that patriarchy is the primary division in society, often rooted in men's control over women's bodies and sexuality?
options: Liberal feminism
Radical feminism
Marxist feminism
Difference feminism
questions.explain: Radical feminists such as Firestone see patriarchy as the primary and universal division, often rooted in the control of women's reproduction and sexuality.

questions.q: In participant observation, a key advantage claimed by interpretivists is:
options: High reliability and easy replication
The production of large statistical samples
The complete absence of ethical issues
High validity through first-hand insight into the group's meanings and way of life
questions.explain: Participant observation offers valid, in-depth understanding of a group from the inside, though it is hard to replicate and may raise ethics issues.

questions.q: Giddens' 'structuration theory' attempts to resolve the structure-action debate by arguing that:
options: Only structure matters
Structure and action are entirely separate
Only agency matters
Structure and agency are a 'duality': structures both constrain action and are reproduced by it
questions.explain: Giddens argued structure and agency are two sides of the same process, as people draw on structures to act and thereby reproduce or change them.

questions.q: Gouldner criticised value-free sociology by arguing that:
options: Claiming to be value-free can mask a conservative bias and a sale of expertise to the powerful
Values are irrelevant to research
Only positivism can be value-laden
All sociology is naturally objective
questions.explain: Gouldner argued that a supposedly value-free sociology often serves established interests, and that committed sociology is preferable.

questions.q: Marxist feminists explain women's oppression primarily by linking patriarchy to:
options: The needs of capitalism, such as unpaid domestic labour reproducing the workforce
Biological differences between the sexes
The interpretivist meaning of housework
An innate male will to dominate
questions.explain: Marxist feminists argue women's unpaid domestic and reproductive labour benefits capitalism by servicing and reproducing the labour force cheaply.

questions.q: Ethnomethodology, founded by Garfinkel, studies:
options: The official statistics of the state
The methods members use to construct a sense of social order in everyday life
The genetic causes of deviance
The economic base of society
questions.explain: Garfinkel's ethnomethodology examines the taken-for-granted methods people use to produce orderly, meaningful social situations.

questions.q: The 'structure versus action' debate in sociology concerns whether:
options: Society should be studied scientifically or not
Human behaviour is shaped by external social forces or by the meanings and choices of individuals
Quantitative data is better than qualitative data
Crime is functional or dysfunctional
questions.explain: Structural theories stress society shaping individuals, while action theories stress individuals creating society through meaningful action.

questions.q: Phenomenology, as developed by Schutz, argues that social order is:
options: Impossible to study at all
Determined solely by economic forces
A product of the shared categories and 'typifications' members use to make sense of the world
Imposed entirely by the state
questions.explain: Schutz argued that we share common-sense typifications that allow us to interpret the world in broadly similar ways, producing social order.

questions.q: A laboratory experiment is rarely used in sociology mainly because:
options: It is artificial, can only study small groups, and raises ethical and validity problems
It is favoured by interpretivists
It is impossible to control any variables
It produces no quantitative data
questions.explain: Lab experiments struggle with the artificiality of settings, the Hawthorne effect and ethics, limiting their use in studying real social life.

questions.q: Max Weber argued that a full sociological explanation of action requires both causal explanation and:
options: 'Verstehen', an empathetic understanding of the actor's subjective meaning
The complete rejection of statistics
The abandonment of objectivity
A focus only on the economic base
questions.explain: Weber combined structural causes with Verstehen, the interpretive understanding of the meanings actors give to their behaviour.
